newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Long end's faith in Fed eroding.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Long end's faith in Fed eroding.

text.p: The short end of the U.S. Treasury market is slowly and reluctantly coming to grips with the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hike short term interest rates soon. Meanwhile, long bond investors are practically screaming for a tightening as soon as possible.

The spread between yields of the 30-year bond and the two-year note widened by a full basis point on Thursday after a larger-than-expected rise in February retail sales, a huge upward revision to January sales and another drop in weekly jobless claims.
The 30-year bond's yield soared to 6.98 percent on Thursday from 6.88 percent on Wednesday. The two-year note's yield jumped to 6.20 percent from 6.11 percent -- a widening of one basis point.

Since the curve is supposed to flatten, not steepen, when the Fed is on the verge of raising rates, analysts said the long end is on the verge of losing confidence that the Fed will be able to keep inflation tame.
"That is the implict message in the selloff at the long end," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
The selloff at the short end clearly suggests that the market expects a tightening. However, a 25 basis point rate hike still is not fully priced in, although it is close.
"By steepening, the market is hinting the Fed should tighten," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.

But he noted that even with the big rises in Treasury yields, the short end still has a little way to go before pricing in a rate hike. He said three-month bills should be 25 basis points below federal funds, six-month bills should be even with funds and year-bills 25 basis points above funds.
At 5.11 percent, the three-month bill is 11 basis points away, while the 5.22 percent six-month bill and 5.43 percent year bill are closer to pricing in a tightening,
"It is clear the market expects (the Fed) to tighten," Liro said. "The whole curve has steepened today. The Fed would read that as a reason to tighten."
However, Liro said the long end still has confidence the Fed will act to control inflation.

"The yield curve has been in such a narrow range -- 65 to 90 basis points -- for more than a year," he said. Once it "breaks out to 100 basis points or higher, then you can make a case that the market is losing a bit of confidence in the Fed's ability to keep down inflation.
"If the Fed doesn't tighten in March, the curve will steepen further," he added. "Then, the market will lose confidence in the Fed."
A tightening, though, would not automatically cause a flattening, since it is unlikely the Fed would stop at just one move, players said.

"If the market fears a tightening, it must price for a sequence of moves over some unspecified period of time," Lieberman said. "(And) even if the Fed tightens policy, it doesn't mean you want to run out and buy long bonds. Even at 7 percent, investors may not be compensated by the (inflation) risks they face."

Yet, John Youngdahl, money market economist at Goldman Sachs & Co, said the market is not telling the Fed to tighten, but the other way around: the strong data and hawkish Fedspeak are forcing the market to believe a tightening is on the horizon.
He said investors have been reluctant to sell longer dated paper, because when they thought the Fed would tighten in 1996, they took a bath when the Fed left rates alone.
"As attitudes of a rate change ratchet up (yields), those who haven't sold are being forced to by a change in their assesements and by the price action," Youngdahl said.
